summary:
Baja California Sur does not criminalise trans people or their presence. The state's elected congress created an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition through a 2021 reform to the state Civil Code, and after the Supreme Court of Mexico ruled in June 2023 that excluding children and adolescents from that procedure was unconstitutional, the congress passed a further Civil Code reform in 2024 extending recognition to children, adolescents and non-binary people.

Human Rights Watch's state-by-state tracker of legal gender recognition in Mexico, dated March 2025, records Baja California Sur among the states that have legislated an administrative procedure, and records the 2024 reform as the one that expanded access to minors and non-binary people following the Supreme Court's June 2023 ruling.

El Financiero reported on 27 June 2024 that the reform approved by the Baja California Sur congress allows minors to change their gender and chosen name on birth certificates, and that the administrative processes are described as rapid, free and free of prejudice for trans and non-binary children. The XVI Legislature worked the dictamen on the order of the Supreme Court's June 2023 ruling, which had struck down the adult-only limit.

For contrast, Human Rights Watch's report of 6 March 2024 on Tabasco, a state with no recognition procedure, documents what the absence of such a procedure produces: institutional mistreatment, the unsolved August 2023 killing of activist Karina Gómez, hate-motivation provisions absent from Tabasco's criminal code, and healthcare staff routinely outting patients by calling legal names. That pattern describes Tabasco, not Baja California Sur, but it indicates what a non-reforming state's trans residents face.

National impunity conditions bear on any visitor's expectation of protection. The Guardian reported on 24 July 2024 that over 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022, and that Mexico City approved the Paola Buenrostro law on 18 July 2024 making transfemicide a crime with sentences up to 70 years, in one of Latin America's deadliest settings for trans people. That law applies to Mexico City, not to Baja California Sur.

Global Affairs Canada advises travellers to exercise a high degree of caution across Mexico because of high levels of criminal activity and kidnapping, with an avoid non-essential travel advisory covering Baja California Sur and the northwestern mainland coast. This is a general-country advisory rather than a trans-specific one.
tangentialFactors:
The Canadian advisory's avoid non-essential travel designation names Baja California Sur directly, but it is issued on criminal-activity and kidnapping grounds rather than on any trans-specific risk, and it applies to all travellers regardless of gender history.

Impunity for homicide in Mexico is documented at above 95% nationally for 2022 (Guardian, 24 July 2024), a figure that shapes how much protection a formal legal right is likely to deliver in practice, including in states that have legislated recognition.

Caroline Beer's analysis of 22 November 2024 for the LSE USAPP found that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, and that rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice; she cautioned explicitly that her earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence including murder and torture. That national finding applies to Baja California Sur's recognition procedure as written.
localsOnly:
Residents of Baja California Sur, including minors and non-binary people, can change gender and chosen name on birth certificates through an administrative procedure created by the 2021 Civil Code reform and expanded by the 2024 reform; El Financiero reported on 27 June 2024 that the processes are rapid, free and free of prejudice.

The state's recognition procedure rests on a state Civil Code reform rather than on a national statute, so its terms are set by the Baja California Sur congress and can be amended by that body.

Same-sex marriage is legal in every Mexican state, so a resident of Baja California Sur in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can marry; adoption rights vary by state.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Baja California Sur-specific incident of violence against a trans person, and no state-level homicide or transfemicide figure for Baja California Sur, is sourced in this inventory; the impunity and killing figures cited here are national or Mexico City figures.

No sourced data is available on how Baja California Sur's prisons house trans prisoners, whether special units or segregation practice exist, or on police conduct toward trans people in this state specifically.

Whether Baja California Sur's administrative recognition procedure has been used, how many applications it has processed, and how long it takes in practice are not sourced; the "rapid, free" description comes from reporting on the reform's text rather than from implementation data.

Whether Baja California Sur's criminal code contains hate-motivation provisions, and whether the state has any anti-discrimination enforcement machinery of its own, are not sourced in this inventory.
